subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Perimenopause

steps.tx: **Perimenopause** spans the biological transition from the late reproductive years through the postmenopause, commencing with initial menstrual cycle variability and concluding twelve months after the final menstrual period. According to the Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop (STRAW+10) staging criteria, perimenopause encompasses stages -2 (early menopausal transition) and -1 (late menopausal transition). The transition typically lasts between four and eight years, driven by progressive exhaustion of the ovarian follicular pool.
steps.say: Perimenopause begins with menstrual cycle irregularities and ends twelve months after the final period. Staged by the STRAW criteria, it typically lasts four to eight years as the ovarian follicular reserve depletes.

vis.alt: Diagram showing endocrine hormonal fluctuations during the perimenopausal transition.
vis.caption: Endocrine transitions in perimenopause: declining inhibin B, fluctuating estradiol, and rising pituitary FSH. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Inhibin B** decline represents the earliest detectable endocrine harbinger of the perimenopausal transition. Produced by healthy granulosa cells of recruited preantral and early antral follicles, inhibin B falls as the primordial follicle pool depletes below critical reserves. The loss of negative feedback selective for follicle-stimulating hormone allows pituitary FSH to rise progressively during the early follicular phase, even while serum estradiol levels remain normal or transiently elevated due to hyperstimulation of remaining follicles.
steps.say: A drop in inhibin B is the first hormonal change of perimenopause. Because inhibin B normally restrains FSH, its decline triggers a compensatory rise in early follicular FSH while estradiol levels fluctuate wildly.

steps.tx: **Menstrual irregularity** constitutes the cardinal clinical hallmark of perimenopause. In the early transition (STRAW stage -2), menstrual cycle length fluctuates by seven days or more between consecutive cycles, often with cycles shortening to twenty-one to twenty-four days due to accelerated follicular phases. In the late transition (STRAW stage -1), cycles skip entirely, marked by two or more skipped cycles and episodes of amenorrhoea lasting sixty days or longer, heralding the approach of the final menses.
steps.say: Early perimenopause causes cycles to vary by seven days or more, often shortening first. Late perimenopause brings skipped cycles and sixty days or more of amenorrhoea, signaling that menopause is near.

steps.tx: **Vasomotor symptoms** represent the most common distressing complaint, affecting up to eighty percent of women during perimenopause. Characterized by sudden, intense sensations of heat spreading across the chest, neck, and face, followed by cutaneous vasodilation, profuse perspiration, and subsequent chilling. Symptoms are driven by rapid fluctuations in circulating estrogen that destabilize central noradrenergic and serotonergic neurotransmission in the preoptic hypothalamus, narrowing the thermoneutral zone and triggering heat-dissipation mechanisms at normal core temperatures.
steps.say: Hot flushes and night sweats affect eighty percent of perimenopausal women. Erratic estrogen drops disrupt hypothalamic thermoreceptors, narrowing the neutral temperature zone and triggering sudden inappropriate sweating.

steps.tx: **Genitourinary syndrome of menopause** encompasses progressive atrophic anatomical changes affecting the labia, clitoris, vagina, urethra, and bladder base resulting from oestrogen receptor deprivation. As vaginal stratified squamous epithelium atrophies, glycogen content plummets, causing depletion of protective hydrogen peroxide-producing lactobacilli and a rise in vaginal pH above 5.0. Patients suffer from vaginal dryness, burning dyspareunia, dysuria, and recurrent urinary tract infections, responding rapidly to low-dose local topical vaginal oestrogens.
steps.say: The genitourinary syndrome of menopause causes vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent urinary infections. Without estrogen, lactobacilli vanish, vaginal pH rises over 5.0, and local topical vaginal estrogens provide targeted relief.

steps.tx: **Contraception guidelines** in perimenopausal women mandate that fertility control must be continued despite irregular menses until permanent menopause is established. Spontaneous, unexpected ovulation can occur even after months of amenorrhoea. Contraception is required for two full years following the last menstrual period in women under fifty years of age, and for one full year in women aged fifty and older. The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is ideal, providing highly effective contraception while controlling heavy perimenopausal bleeding.
steps.say: Perimenopausal women must maintain contraception: continue for two years after the last period if under fifty, or one year if fifty or older. Spontaneous ovulation can still occur despite long stretches of amenorrhoea.

steps.tx: **Systemic hormone replacement therapy** represents the most efficacious treatment for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms and prevention of accelerated postmenopausal bone mineral loss. In women with an intact uterus, systemic estrogen must unconditionally be combined with a progestogen (such as oral micronized progesterone or a levonorgestrel IUS) to prevent unopposed estrogen-induced endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma. In women who have undergone a prior hysterectomy, estrogen-alone therapy is prescribed without progestogen.
steps.say: Hormone replacement therapy is the most effective treatment for hot flushes. If a woman has an intact uterus, always add a progestin to protect against endometrial cancer. Hysterectomized women take estrogen alone.

left.title: Intact Uterus (Combined HRT)

right.title: Prior Hysterectomy (Estrogen Alone)
points: Lower breast cancer risk than combined HRT

steps.tx: **Transdermal estradiol** patches or gels are preferred over oral formulations in perimenopausal women possessing cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity with BMI over thirty, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or elevated risk of venous thromboembolism. Transdermal administration avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism, preventing hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and avoiding elevations in serum triglycerides. Initiating therapy within ten years of menopause in women under age sixty maximizes cardioprotective and bone benefits while minimizing vascular risks.
steps.say: Transdermal estrogen patches bypass the liver, avoiding the rise in clotting factors caused by oral tablets. They are the safest choice for women with obesity, high blood pressure, or elevated thrombosis risk.
